title: Begampura, the city without sorrow
hookLine: Ravidas sings of a city without sorrow, tax or fear, where all walk free (Gauri, Ravidas, ang 345)

lines: A CITY WHERE NO ONE IS AFRAID?
cards: What would a city look like if nobody in it were afraid? No one dreading the tax collector. No one shut out of a street because of their family.

No one first-class and no one second. A leather-worker in Benares, from a family some people kept at the edges, sang about exactly that city, and he gave it a name. It's in the Guru Granth Sahib: Begampura.

teach.b: The hymn is in Raag Gauri, on Ang 345. In paraphrase, Ravidas sings: Begampura is the name of the city. There's no sorrow there and no anxiety.
No tax, no tribute, no property to worry over.

teach.h: NO TAX, NO FEAR, NO RANKING.
teach.b: No fear, no wrongdoing, no dread of decline. I've found a home of my own now, brother, where all is well. The hymn explains its own name: the place where sorrow doesn't live.
Now look at what's missing. Tax and tribute, the things a powerful man could squeeze out of a poor one. Fear.
Ranking. These are weights that press on the poor, and Ravidas builds his city by taking them off, one at a time.

teach.h: NO SECOND OR THIRD; ALL WALK FREE.
teach.b: Then, in paraphrase: the rule there is steady and lasting; there's no second or third, all are one. The people wander freely as they please, and no one stops them.
Hear that, nobody stops them, against yesterday's picture of a family carrying dead cattle through the lanes. The free walking is the point.
At the close Ravidas signs it as one set free, and says, in paraphrase: whoever is a citizen of that city is my friend. Readers hear Begampura in more than one way.

teach.h: THE SOUL'S HOME, OR A TOWN ON EARTH?
teach.b: Some hear the soul's home with the Lord, beyond sorrow.
Others hear a picture of how a town on earth could be, and some carry this hymn into struggles against caste. The hymn holds both. Begampura is a place where no one is second.

how: Ravidas's Begampura hymn is sung in gurdwaras as gurbani, and Sikhs and Ravidassia communities often recall it when speaking of a world without caste or fear.

o: Ravidas's city without sorrow, where no one is second
the gate of Benares where pilgrims paid their tax
the queen's palace in an old capital of the Punjab

games.q: inside the city — tap the pairs.
p: the city where sorrow doesn't live

s: Begampura is a real town on the map of Benares
it's the city Ravidas sings of in Raag Gauri, a city without sorrow.
the hymn says the people there wander freely and no one stops them
they walk as they please, and no one bars the way.

games.q: you're Ravidas, building a city in song for people who were kept at the edges. what do you take away first?
games.why: no sorrow, no anxiety, no tax or tribute, no fear: he takes off the very weights his people carried.

practice: Let a street come to mind, your own or one you know well, and walk it slowly, the way Ravidas walks his city.

Take away one fear the people there carry, then one wall that keeps someone out, then one ranking, and let them move freely, greeting each other, for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Begampura. The city Ravidas names and describes in Raag Gauri: no sorrow, no tax, no fear, no second or third, and everyone walking free.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Begampura, the city without sorrow in Ravidas's hymn.

carryVoice: Your line: the city without sorrow. No second, no third: all are one. Until tomorrow.
